title: Typewriter and Ledger
premise: In the winter of 1914, Beatrix Eastwick drives for the formidable suffragist Lady Vivian Ashcombe, reading every letter she carries and believing history belongs to other people. When the season's first ice closes the bridge to the outside world, a letter arrives naming Lady Vivian's late son's German-born widow, Greta, as heir to the estate — and as an enemy alien to be reported. Bound by a promise made in peacetime, Beatrix hides Greta in the attic while the village turns suspicious, forging documents at the typewriter and cooking the household books to conceal her. As suspicion narrows and the river ice groans toward its spring break, Beatrix must choose between her own safety and the found family she never expected; when the bridge finally opens, she delivers one last letter — her own confession — and claims her place not as a driver of history but as someone it happened to.
about_author: Juniper Halloran is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing letters from English country houses before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted coach house in Yorkshire, where she keeps her grandmother's typewriter on the desk beside a ledger of family debts.

chapters.title: The Last Crossing
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. On the final day before the bridge closes, Beatrix ferries Lady Vivian home through sleet, reading the mail aloud as is their ritual. Among the letters: a solicitor's notice about the late Captain Ashcombe's will. The emotional beat is cozy routine shadowed by unease — Beatrix notices Lady Vivian go very still at one envelope and pocket it unopened.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, with a flashback to 1912. We learn how Beatrix promised the Captain's gentle German wife, Greta, that if ever she needed shelter, the Ashcombe house would open to her. Present-day Lady Vivian burns the solicitor's letter rather than face what it says. Emotional beat: loyalty as inheritance — promises outlive the people who make them.

chapters.title: Enemy Property
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. Greta arrives on foot before the ice fully seals the river, half-frozen, carrying only a valise and her dead husband's letters. Beatrix hides her in the attic above the stables. The beat is fear braided with tenderness: two women who barely know each other bound by a man neither can stop grieving.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. To feed a hidden mouth, Beatrix begins doctoring the household accounts, buying double and writing half. Lady Vivian, sharp-eyed from decades of political warfare, notices the discrepancies but says nothing — yet. The beat is quiet complicity: the typewriter clicks at midnight, and the house becomes a conspiracy of three.

chapters.title: What the Village Saw
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs via village gossip scenes. The postmistress counts cigarette purchases; the constable asks after 'foreign voices.' A suffragist ally, Mrs. Pell, warns Beatrix that war makes neighbors into informants. Emotional beat: paranoia seeping into a community, and Beatrix realizing history has been happening here all along.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. In the attic, Greta reads aloud her husband's wartime letters, which Lady Vivian has never been able to open. Mother-in-law and widow meet properly for the first time across a candlelit table. The beat is grief shared becoming grief halved — and Lady Vivian, the suffragist, confronting that her cause never included women like Greta.

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The constable arrives with a warrant list of enemy aliens; Lady Vivian stalls him with imperious charm while Beatrix moves Greta into the hidden priest hole behind the linen press. The beat is terror and exhilaration — Beatrix discovers she is braver than she believed, and that courage, like the bridge, once crossed cannot be uncrossed.

chapters.title: Ice Breaking
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. Mrs. Pell is arrested for her suffrage record and, under pressure, mentions 'the German girl.' The river ice cracks audibly; spring is coming, and with it the reopening of the road and the end of hiding. Greta decides to surrender herself rather than destroy the household. Beat: sacrifice offered freely, love declared without romance.

chapters.title: The Confession
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, climax. At the tribunal convened in the village hall, Beatrix stands before magistrates and villagers and confesses everything — the forged ledgers, the false names, the promise — claiming authorship of the crime so Greta's case becomes mercy's case. Lady Vivian rises to testify. The beat is the book's thesis made flesh: ordinary people stepping into history.

chapters.title: Typewriter and Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, resolution. Greta is released to Lady Vivian's guardianship pending appeal; Beatrix pays a fine and loses her position — and is immediately rehired, by Greta, as secretary to the newly reopened estate school for local girls. On the repaired bridge, Beatrix posts her last letter: her own account of the winter. Beat: identity claimed, family chosen, history owned.
